newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian anthrax outbreak threatens dairy exports.
newsitem.headline: Australian anthrax outbreak threatens dairy exports.

text.p: Australia's worst outbreak of the cattle disease anthrax in decades is threatening A$1.8 billion (US$1.4 billion) in dairy product exports and has taken the unusual turn of infecting an abattoir worker.
Dairy industry and government officials on Wednesday were shaken by the rapid spread of the disease in recent days, with 68 animals killed on about 31 farms in the state of Victoria.
A 40-year-old abattoir worker has been hospitalised and is undergoing a penicillin treatment, said Dr Rosemary Lester of the Victoria's public health department.
Lester said the unnamed abattoir employee, from a yard which handled animals with the disease, now has no symptoms.
The cause of the anthrax outbreak is not known, but the disease usually appears following rain and hot, humid weather -- conditions Victoria has recently experienced.
Anthrax, a bacterial infection, causes rapid death in cattle, sheep and goats which eat contaminated material. It rarely affects humans but can be contracted through a small cut or scratch.
Officials say the worst of the outbreak appears to have been contained by the vaccination of 9,000 cattle on 94 properties and the quarantining of infected farms.
But with finicky Asian markets now the biggest customers for Australian exports of milk powder, butter, cheese, milk and other products, the local industry waits with concern for the impact on sales.
David Loutit, chief executive officer of the Victorian Dairy Industry Authority, said that only "fairly minor" effects on exports were expected.
"Obviously it's a serious matter (but) from everything we hear people (know) the matter is under control and the product is safe," Loutit said.
The dairy chief's statement was despite fresh memories of a Japanese consumer boycott of imported beef during last year's "Mad Cow" disease outbreak in Britain.
Initial reactions from exporters connected with servicing the sensitive Japanese market were not encouraging.
Rejection by Japanese customers of Australian dairy products would create a "virtually immediate" effect on exports, a Japanese trading house official said.
It was feared the notoriously jittery Japanese market would see the anthrax threat as Australia-wide and disregard the fact that processing eliminated the threat of infection, he said.
"Obviously Tokyo is quite anxious to see if the problem will have an overall effect on the market," the trader said.
Australian dairy products are sold around the world, with Japan, the Philippines, Malaysia, Thailand and other customers in Asia forming the biggest market, ahead of the Middle East and Europe.

Although isolated instances of anthrax occasionally occur, the Victorian outbreak covers an area which supplies about 30 percent of Australia's dairy products. Victoria as a whole produces about 50 percent of Australia's total diary product.
"We're hopeful its (the anthrax outbreak) under control," Steve Tate, senior veterinary officer of Victoria's Department of Natural Resources and Energy, told Reuters.
But a return to hot, humid, rain-soaked conditions could bring new outbreaks, said officials.
